item.title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
item.description: arXiv:2610.20889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~\mu\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.
item.dc:creator: Tai Xiang, Yue-Hui Lu, Tsai-Chen Lee, Jacquelyn Ho, Michael Lan, Zhenjie Yan, Harry Levine, Nathaniel B. Vilas, Dan M. Stamper-Kurn

item.title: Fast, parallel, three-dimensional rearrangement of atom arrays using superpositions of elementary holograms
item.description: arXiv:2610.21609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assembling defect-free arrays of neutral atoms requires real-time rearrangement of stochastically loaded optical tweezers. Conventional rearrangement methods shuttle atoms sequentially, whereas high-speed spatial light modulators (SLMs) can move all atoms in parallel, which scales more favorably as the array size grows. For fast parallel rearrangement, the sequence of holograms displayed on the SLM should be computed more rapidly than the SLM refresh rate, and there should be phase continuity between successive holograms to minimize transient intensity fluctuations. We calculate holograms analytically by adding together the complex fields needed to produce each individual trap, and we ramp the phase of each trap linearly as it moves to its target location. Trap positions enter as continuous variables, rather than tied to points on a grid, so the method provides high positioning accuracy. Using a single GPU, we compute each intermediate hologram in 0.284 ms, considerably faster than the SLM refresh time of 0.696 ms, so the rearrangement speed is hardware-limited. In each step, we use the free processing time to iteratively optimize the holograms for equal intensity across the traps, decreasing trap non-uniformity to 1.24% during rearrangement at no cost in total time. Starting from an array of 256 sites loaded stochastically with $^{87}$Rb atoms, we assemble a 100-atom array in under 20 ms with a rearrangement survival probability of 99.31(12)% per atom. This rearrangement increases the temperature of the atoms by 9(3) $\mu$K, which is small compared to the trap depth of 480 $\mu$K. Our method can also move individual atoms axially, enabling transport in different planes. We demonstrate this capability with a rearrangement protocol where one set of atoms leapfrogs over another.
item.dc:creator: D. J. Hoare, P. Dunniece, J. Rodewald, K. K. Voges, M. R. Tarbutt

item.title: A QED Functional Formulation of Relativistic Many-Body Perturbation Theory in Atoms
item.description: arXiv:2610.22216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We systematically derive relativistic many-body perturbation theory (RMBPT) from the two-particle irreducible effective action of quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the Furry picture, giving an organisational and diagrammatic framework for both correlation and radiative corrections in many-electron atoms. We further discuss that RMBPT is a well-defined subset of QED effects evaluated on a redefined vacuum, such that the interplay between correlation and radiative effects becomes transparent. We use this to derive QED corrections to the interelectronic interaction of atomic systems, yielding the transverse (frequency-dependent Breit) photon-exchange corrections, including retardation. Of those corrections, we numerically evaluate the first-order transverse photon-exchange corrections, which complement the conventional RMBPT based on the Dirac-Coulomb no-pair Hamiltonian.
item.dc:creator: Cedric de Jonge, Zolt\'an Harman

item.title: Projected sensitivity of a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate comagnetometer to proton monopole-dipole interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.22346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Light spin-zero bosons with scalar and pseudoscalar couplings mediate a parity- and time-reversal-violating monopole-dipole interaction between unpolarized matter and polarized spins. For proton spins, the interaction has been probed directly only at ranges $\lambda \gtrsim$ 5 mm; below this range, laboratory limits are inferred from neutron-dominated nuclei through nuclear-spin models. We analyze a direct search with a single-domain $^{87}$Rb spinor Bose-Einstein condensate in close proximity to a source mass. The F=1 and F=2 manifolds act as two co-located magnetometers that precess in opposite directions in a magnetic field but in the same direction under the exotic interaction. They thus form a natural comagnetometer, in which the sum of their precession angles suppresses field noise by a measured 44 dB and a weighted sum cancels the field altogether. Taking as a starting point the demonstrated magnetometry [Palacios et al. Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. \textbf{119}, e2115339119 (2022)] and comagnetometry [Gomez et al. Phys. Ref. Lett. \textbf{124}, 170401 (2020)] performance of the $^{87}$Rb single-domain spinor condensate at ICFO [Palacios et al. New J. Phys. \textbf{20}, 053008 (2018)], we study the projected sensitivity as a function of source-mass geometry and in-progress improvements to atom loading methods, trap beam geometry, and magnetic environment. With an insulating bismuth germanate source mass with a spherical top, whose apex sits 50 $\mu$m below the center of the condensate, one week of acquisition would reach $|g_s^N g_p^p|\approx 2\times10^{-22}$ with these upgrades and $3\times10^{-24}$ at the projection-noise limit ($\lambda=100\, \mu$m, 95\% C.L.). This is more than three and five orders of magnitude below existing laboratory limits. The improvement covers boson masses of 0.3-50 meV/c$^2$ after the upgrades and 0.09-70 meV/c$^2$ at the projection-noise limit.
item.dc:creator: Wenjing Zhou, Diego Blas, Morgan W. Mitchell

item.title: A tutorial on quantum scattering theory and coupled-channel calculations of bimolecular collisions
item.description: arXiv:2610.20882v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collisions between atoms and molecules govern how energy is exchanged and redistributed in the gas phase, underpinning phenomena from spectral line broadening and interstellar molecular excitation to the cooling and trapping of molecules. A quantitative account of these collisions requires connecting the theoretical description of the interaction between the collision partners to measurable quantities such as cross sections. However, scattering theory as presented in quantum mechanics textbooks does not readily translate into numerical methods. Here, we formulate the scattering problem in Dirac notation, as customary in present-day quantum mechanics courses, and show how to build a practical numerical framework from it. We derive the "coupled channel" representation of the scattering problem with correct asymptotic behaviour and introduce Numerov's method to obtain time-independent wavefunctions, from which we calculate cross sections, the observables measured in scattering experiments. Starting from single channel scattering, we build up to the realistic collision of a ground-state atom with a diatomic molecule.
item.dc:creator: Karl P. Horn, Christiane P. Koch

item.title: Simulation of topological superconductors and their competing orders using photon-mediated interactions
item.description: arXiv:2512.17889v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Realizing and controlling the unconventional pairing featured by topological superconductors remains a central challenge. We introduce a cavity QED quantum simulator that engineers competing chiral $p_x+ip_y$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}+id_{xy}$ orders by tailoring cavity-mediated couplings between atomic pseudospins that emulate momentum-dependent pairing channels. The desired spatially inhomogeneous cavity-mediated couplings can be engineered in a 2D optical lattice using incommensurate cavity-lattice wavelengths naturally occurring in cavity QED systems. This minimal and fully tunable platform enables controlled state preparation and continuous measurement of superconducting order parameters. To probe this competition, the platform enables selective excitation and direct time-domain detection of Bardasis-Schrieffer modes---collective excitations of the subdominant pairing channel. The same competing channel can have an even stronger impact out of equilibrium, where a sudden quench can drive its growth and abruptly reshape the dominant superconducting order, despite the stability of the dominant order in equilibrium. Together, these results establish cavity QED as a controlled setting for revealing hidden competing orders and exploring nonlinear dynamics of topological superconductivity that remain elusive in solid-state and ultracold-atom systems.
item.dc:creator: Anjun Chu, Joyce Kwan, Eric Yilun Song, Seth Hew Peng Chew, James K. Thompson, Ana Maria Rey

item.title: Realization of a cavity-coupled Rydberg array
item.description: arXiv:2602.12152v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scalable quantum computers and quantum networks require the combination of quantum processing nodes with efficient light-matter interfaces to distribute quantum information in local or long-distance quantum networks. Neutral-atom arrays have both been coupled to Rydberg states to enable high-fidelity quantum gates in universal processing architectures, and to optical cavities to realize interfaces to photons. However, combining these two capabilities and coupling atom arrays to highly excited Rydberg states in the mode of an optical cavity has been an outstanding challenge. Here we present a novel cavity-coupled Rydberg array that achieves this long-standing goal. We prepare, detect, and control individual atoms in a scalable optical tweezer array, couple them strongly to the optical mode of a high-finesse optical cavity and excite them in a controlled way to Rydberg states. We show that high-cooperativity coupling to an optical cavity -- demonstrated via the dispersive shift of the resonance of the cavity in presence of the atoms -- and strong Rydberg interactions -- demonstrated via the collective enhancement of Rydberg coupling in the atomic array -- can be achieved in our setup at the same spatial location. Our presented experimental platform opens the path to several new directions, including the realization of quantum network nodes, quantum simulation of long-range interacting, open quantum systems and photonic-state engineering leveraging high-fidelity Rydberg control.
item.dc:creator: Jacopo De Santis, Bal\'azs Dura-Kov\'acs, Mehmet \"Onc\"u, Adrien Bouscal, Dimitrios Vasileiadis, Johannes Zeiher

item.title: Simulating cavity QED with spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensates revisited
item.description: arXiv:2603.28368v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating cavity quantum electrodynamics in synthetic platforms offers a route to studying light--matter physics without real photons. We reassess the frequently invoked analogy between harmonically trapped, spin--orbit-coupled atoms and the quantum Rabi and Dicke models, with particular emphasis on squeezing and entanglement. A single non-interacting atom realizes the quantum Rabi Hamiltonian exactly, up to elementary spin and phase-space rotations. For $N$ non-interacting atoms, however, the center-of-mass mode is only one member of a complete orthonormal set containing $N-1$ relative modes. We prove that, after all modes are included, the spin--spin terms generated by the collective mode cancel exactly against those generated by the relative modes. Equivalently, the original Hamiltonian is a sum of independent one-particle Hamiltonians and therefore cannot create interparticle entanglement from a separable state. Contact interactions invalidate this cancellation but do not remove the relative modes or turn the exact many-body Hamiltonian into a Dicke model. A one-mode Dicke description can arise only as a controlled low-energy approximation after all relevant relative excitations have been shown to be spectrally suppressed. We discuss this distinction together with experimental scales, finite temperature, and possible mode-selection strategies. We also distinguish the single-particle interference underlying density fringes from the interaction-stabilized stripe supersolid observed in many-body condensates.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad S. Hasan, Karol Gietka
